messages.author: 945a91d0fe28fce8
messages.subject: Poisson model running slowly
parts:
Hi, I'm a novice user of Stan and mainly use Winbugs (and SAS) for Bayesian modeling.  A current model I have takes about 9 hours to run in Winbugs and I am excited about Stan possibility reducing the run time down substantially.  Perhaps my questions is trivial but I have tried several methods and can't seem to get it to work as I wish.  I have included my model below and this model runs fine and I have compared the model results to Winbugs and results are similar.  However, the model runs slowly and is much slower than Winbugs but I believe I know why and have been trying to recode without success.  For the code below under transformed parameters I'm computing the linear predictor and mean for each observation and I have no use at this time for these individual level predictions as I'm only interested in the estimated parameters.  I've tried recoding so it would fit the model without estimating the LP and mu for each observation as I believe this is what's causing Stan to run slowly.  Any ideas or help is greatly appreciated, thanks, chuck 


// Poisson model example
 
 data {
   // Define variables in data
   // Number of observations (an integer)
   int<lower=0> N;
   // Number of beta parameters
   int<lower=0> p;
 
   // Covariates
   real intercept[N];
   real drug[N];
   real dist[N];
   real cap[N];
   real unemp[N];
   real white[N];
   real income[N];
  
 
   // offset
   real offset[N];
  
   // Count outcome
   int<lower=0> y[N];
 }
 
 parameters {
   // Define parameters to estimate
   real beta[p];
 }
 
 transformed parameters  {
   //
   real lp[N];
   real <lower=0> mu[N];
 
   for (i in 1:N) {
     // Linear predictor
     lp[i] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*drug[i] + beta[3]*dist[i] + beta[4]*cap[i] + beta[5]*unemp[i] + beta[6]*white[i]+ beta[7]*income[i] + offset[i];
 
     // Mean
     mu[i] <- exp(lp[i]);
   }
 }
 
 model {
   // Prior part of Bayesian inference
  
 
   // Likelihood part of Bayesian inference
   y ~ poisson(mu);
 }

messages.author: 4e90fa9f1b035969
messages.subject: Re: Poisson model running slowly
parts:
Two quick thoughts: 

1) The exponentiation to get mu is not really necessary. You can use the log expectation with the poisson_log() function. 

2) You could multiply a design matrix by your parameter vector and use vector addition to add the offset (log_mu <- X * beta + offset) instead of doing element-wise summation in the loop. Then you can pass log_mu directly into the poisson_log() function.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson model running slowly
parts:
Declare your covariates as a matrix

matrix[N,M] x;

That is, x[n,1] = drug[n], ... And declare your
coeffs as a vector

vector[M] beta;

with intercept

real alpha;

and then code your model as

y ~ poisson_log(x * beta + intercept + alpha);

This should make it a bit faster per iteration, but won't
change the posterior. I'm a bit confused by the naming, because
you have a constant precomputed intercept --- is that just an
offset by the data mean of y? If so, you could calculate that
in the model as transformed data and it'd be more self-contained
and reliable (no chance of error passing in mismatched data).

What you may need to do is provide some kind of prior on
the coefficients alpha and beta.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson model running slowly
parts:
Also, what are you comparing? You need to use effective sample size per second
computed with Stan's notion of n_eff, which is more conservative than the one used
in JAGS or WinBUGS. And you have to run multiple chains to make sure they're exploring
the same posterior to diagnose convergence.

Also, you didn't say what you thought the problem was. If it's
just storing all those output predictors, my previous message solves
that problem.

- Bob
